cards.title: Subcubic weighted Gomory–Hu trees
cards.formal: Historical question, resolved affirmatively: can an exact Gomory–Hu tree of an undirected integer-weighted graph on \(n\) vertices be constructed in truly subcubic time in \(n\), with polylogarithmic dependence on the largest capacity? The 2022 theorem gives a randomized \(\widetilde O(n^{2})\)-time construction. The 2025 theorem further gives deterministic almost-linear time in the number of edges when capacities are polynomially bounded.

cards.definitions:
The input is an explicitly represented undirected graph \(G=(V,E,w)\), with \(n\geq2\) named vertices and nonnegative integer edge capacities written in binary. Write \(W=\max(1,\max_{e\in E}w(e))\). The standard weighted representation stores at most one total capacity for each unordered vertex pair, so \(m=|E|\leq\binom n2\). Parallel edges can be combined by summing their capacities, with the time to read the original list included. Loops and zero-capacity edges do not affect cuts.

For \(S\subseteq V\), its cut capacity is
\[\delta_{G}(S)=\sum_{\{u,v\}\in E:\,|\{u,v\}\cap S|=1}w(\{u,v\}).\]
For distinct \(s,t\in V\), the minimum separating cut value is \(\lambda_{G}(s,t)=\min_{S:\,s\in S,\ t\notin S}\delta_{G}(S)\). By max-flow/min-cut duality, this is also the maximum flow value between the pair.

A Gomory–Hu tree is a weighted tree \(T\) on exactly the vertex set \(V\), with \(n-1\) edges. For every distinct pair \(s,t\), the smallest edge weight on the unique tree path from \(s\) to \(t\) must equal \(\lambda_{G}(s,t)\). In addition, removing a minimum-weight edge on that path must give a partition that is an actual minimum \(s,t\) cut of \(G\), with that capacity. Thus the output represents both cut values and cut partitions, not just a table of pairwise numbers.

The tree need not be a subgraph of \(G\), and its edge weights need not be weights of individual input edges. Capacities, cut values and tree weights are exact. A tree that approximates pairwise cuts by a multiplicative factor does not satisfy this output requirement. Disconnected components can be joined by zero-weight tree edges, so connectivity is not an essential promise.

Truly subcubic means an upper bound \(O(n^{3-\eta}\operatorname{polylog}(nW))\) for some fixed \(\eta>0\). All input reading, construction and output costs are included. In particular, for \(W=n^{O(1)}\), logarithmic factors can be absorbed into a smaller positive exponent saving. The integer-capacity regime and dependence on its representation follow the resolving work; no bound independent of the number of bits in arbitrary real weights is asserted.

The original question permits randomization. A Monte Carlo construction must output a correct exact tree with high probability on every input; failure probability refers to the algorithm's internal randomness, not a random graph distribution. A deterministic construction always gives a correct tree. The 2022 randomized guarantee already answers the historical question; derandomization is additional progress.

The notation \(\widetilde O\) in the 2022 theorem suppresses polylogarithmic factors in \(n\) and \(W\). The later deterministic bound is \(m^{1+o(1)}\) on nontrivial connected instances with polynomially bounded integer capacities, or \((m+n)^{1+o(1)}\) when explicitly accounting for isolated vertices and component handling. The almost-linear guarantee is not asserted here for arbitrarily large capacities.
cards.answer_criterion: The required affirmative answer is a construction algorithm with exact cut equivalence, a uniform truly subcubic running-time bound in the specified capacity model, and its correctness guarantee. The published randomized 2022 theorem provides this. Computing only a global minimum cut, only one source’s cut values, or an approximate cut tree would not suffice.

context_blocks.title: The compact representation was known long before a fast construction
context_blocks.text: Gomory and Hu proved existence of a cut-equivalent tree and constructed one using at most one fewer single-pair max-flow call than the number of vertices. Even a nearly linear individual flow routine leaves a cubic dense-graph cost in that construction.

context_blocks.title: The weighted cubic barrier was broken
context_blocks.text: Theorem 1.3 gives a randomized nearly quadratic algorithm for general integer-weighted graphs. The following remarks explicitly say that it does not assume an unproved near-linear max-flow algorithm. The result produces the cut tree itself.

context_blocks.title: Deterministic construction subsequently became almost linear
context_blocks.text: The 2025 Theorem 1.1 obtains an \(m^{1+o(1)}\)-time deterministic construction for polynomially bounded integer weights. The capacity restriction is part of the theorem and is kept here rather than inferred away from its shorter abstract.

context_blocks.title: A comparison with shortest paths is a separate conditional consequence
context_blocks.text: The original motivation contrasts all-pairs maximum flow with all-pairs shortest paths. The algorithmic upper bound for cut trees is unconditional; claiming a strict complexity separation additionally requires the relevant shortest-path hardness hypothesis.

meta.status_scope: No claim of exhaustive open-status verification
methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.

Selection groups follow the agreed 10 large and 25 small categories. Our primary goal is a benchmark of 500 problems. Top 100 is a priority subset of those same 500, with secondary editorial attention. Both use the same category order and the same ranking within each category. The existing Top 1000 view is not an active benchmark goal. The respective prefixes are 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 problems per large/small category. The legacy Top 1000 view has 1000 assigned places and 0 reserved places. Each card records its category explicitly. These counts describe saved candidates; classification does not verify a statement or its current open status. Deleted records are absent from the catalogue and exports. Their stable IDs and reasons are retained to prevent reimport. Final quota selection and a comprehensive deduplication audit remain pending.

Importance ordering is an editorial assessment of foundational significance, breadth of consequences, and influence on other questions. Each assessed card gives a reason. The category-wide review also uses shared priority bands for questions of comparable scope; it does not claim that these ties have a scientifically meaningful internal order. Unassessed drafts share a provisional score of 50; their relative order is only an ID tie-break, not an importance judgment. The first 5/2 places in each large/small category are an explicit editorial focus selection balancing importance and topical diversity. Focus ordering does not alter importance scores; remaining candidates use score and ID order. The primary target is 500 problems; Top 100 is its priority subset with secondary editorial attention. Top 100, Top 500 and the legacy Top 1000 view use the first 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 category places respectively, all from the same ranking. Category positions include all candidates and remain fixed when filtering. Publication date, source date, and card detail do not increase importance. Records marked resolved are placed after the remaining candidates, without changing their historical importance score. Importance review does not establish that a saved question is still open.

benchmark_selection.basis: Individual editorial review of saved titles, importance rationales, problem statements, source notes and working summaries. This is a review of importance and topical diversity, not a fresh verification of open status or completion of draft formulations. Importance scores are preserved.
